unit.title: Perform advanced welding using flux cored arc welding process - FCAW

summary: This Level 3 unit takes flux-cored arc welding (FCAW) beyond flat and horizontal work. You will learn to choose between gas-shielded and self-shielded wires and read their classifications, set up for all-position and multi-pass work, weld thick plate, pipe and large fillets to a WPS, back gouge, prevent hydrogen cracking, solidification cracking and lamellar tearing, inspect and repair welds, estimate wire, gas and time, and lead an FCAW crew.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). At Level 2 you learned to weld with flux-cored wire in the flat and horizontal positions. Here you weld **thick plate, pipe and large fillets in all positions**, to a welding procedure specification (WPS), and you choose the wire, plan the passes, inspect the work and lead others.

FCAW is the main production process in many Jamaican structural and plant fabrication shops: building frames, crane and bridge girders, tanks, hoppers, trailers and the repair of quarry, sugar and bauxite plant. It lays down weld metal faster than stick welding, and self-shielded wires work outdoors in the wind.
**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and FCAW welders moving into coded structural work, pipe work or charge-hand roles.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means on the job
rows: Read FCAW classifications and choose rutile, basic, self-shielded, low-alloy or stainless wires for the job and the WPS.
Control fume (manganese, and chromium from stainless), arc light, noise from slag removal, heavy spools and site conditions.
Set polarity, drive rolls, contact tip, stick-out, gas flow and settings within the WPS, and check them at the first piece.
Read welding symbols; prepare and fit single- and double-V butts, large fillets and pipe joints.
Make multi-pass groove and fillet welds in 2G, 3G, 4G, 2F, 3F and pipe positions, with the right bead order and gun angles.
Control hydrogen, preheat (tacks too), interpass temperature, bead shape and restraint; recognise lamellar tearing.
Gouge to sound metal, inspect by eye, MT or PT and macro, and repair faults so the repair can be accepted.
Work out weld metal, wire, gas, arc time and labour; control quality across a crew; keep records.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on wire types, wire care, cracking, pipe, multi-pass and fillet technique, back gouging, health and safety, process choice, calculations, drawings, inspection and leading the team.

A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms such as needle scaler, PB, carbon dioxide, CVN, hardfacing, build-up) and essays that compare wires, explain cracking, or describe a joint, a repair or an estimate.

**Practical tasks**: a double-V full-penetration butt in the 2G position with back gouging, plus a multi-pass 2F fillet, with macro sections; and a pipe joint with a GTAW or GMAW root and FCAW fill and cap in the 5G position.

blocks.note: Many questions ask which wire, which technique or which check is **best for a given job**. Learn the reasons in the comparison tables, not just the names.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Point
Gas-shielded (FCAW-G)
Self-shielded (FCAW-S)
rows: The flux plus a shielding gas: CO2, or an argon-CO2 mix
The flux alone: it makes its own gas and slag, so no cylinder
Windy sites, wharves, towers, field repairs
Smooth arc, little spatter, good-looking bead
Harsher arc; more spatter and fume
Most types DCEN (electrode negative); some DCEP
Often longer, about 20–40 mm or more, exactly as the maker gives
Stick-out too short or too long; mixing its weld metal with other processes

blocks.h: Reading a carbon steel FCAW classification

head: Part
Meaning
In E71T-1C
rows: Minimum tensile strength of the weld metal, in units of 10 000 psi
Positions: 0 = flat and horizontal only; 1 = all positions
Usability: the type of flux, the polarity and how the wire behaves
1: rutile type, DCEP, single and multi-pass
Shielding gas the wire was classified with: C = 100% CO2; M = argon mix (about 75–80% argon, the rest CO2); no letter = self-shielded

blocks.p: Extra marks follow: **-J** shows improved toughness at a lower temperature, and **H4, H8 or H16** gives the most diffusible hydrogen in ml per 100 g of weld metal. Newer packaging may show a longer code under a newer AWS standard, but the same facts (strength, positions, usability, gas, toughness, hydrogen) are still there; ask your instructor to show you.

head: Type
Shielding and polarity
Character
Typical use
rows: Smooth spray-like arc, fast-freezing slag that holds the pool; all-position types available; higher hydrogen and less toughness than T-5
General structural and plant work in all positions
Lime-type slag; low hydrogen; very tough, crack-resistant weld metal; more globular arc and runnier slag, so harder out of position
Thick, highly restrained joints; crane girders; low-temperature work
Structural site work that needs impact toughness
High deposit, shallow penetration; flat and horizontal only; no toughness rating
Heavy non-critical fill in the flat position
High deposit; flat and horizontal types and all-position types
General purpose; the maker limits plate thickness; no toughness rating
Light structural and general work on thinner steel

blocks.note: Only the wire class the WPS names goes on the job. A wire that 'runs smoother' or 'is what the store had' is a change to the procedure.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Low-alloy wires carry an alloy code after the class. **Ni1** means about 1% nickel, added for toughness at low temperatures, as in **E81T1-Ni1C** (80 000 psi minimum).
Bridges and structures of **weathering steel**, which is left unpainted and forms its own protective rust, need a wire whose weld metal weathers to match, as the WPS names.

Stainless wires use the stainless grade number: **E308LT1** joins 304 stainless to 304; **E316LT1** joins 316 to 316; **E309LT1** joins stainless to carbon steel, because its extra chromium and nickel can take the dilution from the carbon steel and still give a sound stainless weld. The ending -1 or -4 shows the gas (CO2 or argon mix).
Keep brushes, grinding discs and clamps for stainless separate from carbon steel tools.

head: Compared with
Why FCAW is often chosen
When it is not
rows: Continuous wire: no electrode changes; lays more metal per hour; deeper penetration; less stopping and starting
Small repairs, very awkward access, no wire feeder available
Slag holds the pool for all-position work; better on mill scale; self-shielded types work in wind
Thin sheet; where slag removal is a problem; open pipe roots
Long, flat seams on thick plate, where SAW is faster

ul: Flux-cored wire picks up moisture through its seam, which adds hydrogen and causes porosity. Keep spools sealed until needed and store them in a dry, warm store.
Do not leave a spool on the feeder overnight in a humid shop or site container: cover it or take it off and bag it, as the maker says.
Re-dry a spool **only if the maker's instructions allow it**, at the temperature they give; many makers say damp cored wire is scrapped.
Rusty wire feeds badly and adds porosity: use a clean spool.
Keep spools of different classes apart and labelled, so the wrong class cannot be picked up.

blocks.p: FCAW makes more fume than solid-wire welding, and self-shielded wires make the most. The fume contains metal oxides from the wire and flux.

head: Fume
Why it matters
Control
rows: Long exposure harms the nervous system, with shaking, slow movement and mood changes, similar to Parkinson's disease
Local exhaust ventilation at the arc or a fume-extraction gun; head out of the plume; respirator where the assessment says
Harms the lungs and can cause cancer
Local extraction always; the respirator the risk assessment names; never in an enclosed bay without both
Metal fume fever: flu-like illness a few hours later
Grind the coating off the weld area; extraction; respirator
Coughing, irritation, lung damage over years; CO2 can build up in low, enclosed places

ul: **Arc light:** FCAW runs at high currents. Typical shades are about 11 up to about 200 A and 12–13 above, from the chart. Screen the bay.
**Spatter and slag:** wear flame-resistant clothing, with trousers **over** the boot tops so spatter cannot drop in, and leather sleeves or a jacket for vertical and overhead work.
**Noise:** needle scalers, grinders and gouging are loud; wear hearing protection when using them, especially for long periods.
**Heavy spools:** 15 kg spools on booms or feeders above head height need a step platform, or the feeder lowered; never stand on the welding machine.
**Electric shock:** dry PPE; the gun and wire are live whenever the trigger is pressed.
Wind on wharves, hilltops and open sites blows away shielding gas, causing porosity. Screen the joint, or use a self-shielded wire **that the WPS covers**. Turning the gas up does not fix it.
Heat and humidity: keep wire covered, take breaks and drink water, and keep machines in the shade.
Rain: stop welding and cover joints and equipment; wet joints add hydrogen.

blocks.note: On galvanised steel, hot-dip coatings are common on Jamaican tower, fence and canopy steel. Grind the zinc off at least 25 mm each side of the joint before welding, use extraction, and repair the coating afterwards as the specification says.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Item
Check
rows: As the wire label and WPS say: DCEP for most gas-shielded wires; DCEN for most self-shielded wires. Wrong polarity gives spatter, a rough arc and poor penetration
**Knurled** rolls (or the maker's cored-wire rolls) of the right size, with **light** pressure. Smooth V rolls or too much pressure crush the tube, open its seam and spill flux
Liner clean and the right size; contact tip the size of the wire and not worn oval
As the maker and WPS give. Too short on self-shielded wire causes porosity; too long gives a cold, unstable arc
Right gas for the wire class; flow typically about 15–25 L/min, checked **at the nozzle** with a flowmeter, because a leaking hose or gun cuts the flow; nozzle clean
Wire feed speed (which sets the current) and voltage within the WPS ranges; checked on a test piece
On clean metal near the joint
Working, placed close to the arc

blocks.p: CO2 is stored as a liquid. On a long run at high flow, the gas boils off so fast that it cools the cylinder and regulator, which can **frost up and freeze**, and the flow drops or stops. Use a heated CO2 regulator, or draw from several cylinders on a manifold, as the supplier advises.

head: Change
Effect
rows: More current, more deposit, deeper penetration
Longer arc; wider, flatter bead. Too much: spatter, undercut, porosity. Too little: wire stubs into the plate; tall, humped bead
Less current at the same wire feed speed; less penetration
Smaller bead; less penetration; risk of undercut and lack of fusion
Larger wire (for example 1.6 mm instead of 1.2 mm)
More deposit per hour, but a bigger pool that is harder to hold out of position

blocks.note: For all-position work on plate of about 10–12 mm, 1.2 mm wire is often chosen over 1.6 mm, because its smaller pool is easier to hold in the vertical and overhead positions.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: On a run of identical parts, check the **first one fully** (settings measured at the arc, bead size and shape, fit-up, and a quick inspection) before the rest are welded. A fault found on the first part costs one repair; found on the last, it may cost twenty.

sections.title: Joint design, fit-up and welding symbols

head: Point
Single-V
Double-V
rows: About half as much at the same angle (less wire, less time)
More angular distortion: all the shrinkage is on one side
Less: welding the sides in turn balances the shrinkage
Both sides must be reached; the plate may need turning
Welded from one side, often onto backing
Root of the first side back gouged from the second side

blocks.p: For a double-V with the root face in the middle, the depth of each V = (plate thickness − root face) ÷ 2. For 25 mm plate with a 3 mm root face, each V is 11 mm deep.

ul: Check bevel angles, root face, gap and alignment against the WPS before tacking.
Tacks are made to the WPS, with preheat if the WPS gives one.
Pre-set double-V plates slightly where the WPS or the instructor says, so the joint pulls flat.
On beams, **weld access holes** (rat holes) are cut in the web where the flanges are butt welded, so the flange weld can be made right across without a break, and back gouged and inspected.

head: Part of the symbol
What it tells you
rows: The line the weld symbol sits on
Weld on the **arrow side** (the side the arrow touches)
Number to the left of the symbol
Weld size (for a fillet, the leg length)
Numbers to the right, such as 50-150
Intermittent welds: each 50 mm long, at 150 mm pitch (centre to centre)
Circle at the bend of the arrow
Flag at the bend of the arrow
Field weld: made on site, not in the shop
Extra information, such as the process or the WPS number to use

ul: The **leg** is measured from the root to the toe on each plate; the **throat** is the shortest distance from the root to the face. On a flat-faced fillet with equal legs, the throat is about 0.7 × the leg.
A very **concave** face may leave the throat too small even when the legs are to size. A very **convex** face wastes metal, traps slag between passes and leaves sharp toes.
Where the drawing shows it, fillets are **returned** (carried round the corner) at the ends of brackets and stiffeners, so the weld does not stop at a corner where cracks start.
Doubling the leg size gives **four times** the weld metal, because the area is leg × leg ÷ 2. Never over-weld.
**Drag** the gun (point it back at the pool) about 10–15° so the slag stays **behind** the pool. Slag that runs ahead gets trapped.
Clean **all** slag after every pass, especially at the toes, with a chipping hammer, wire brush or needle scaler. Grind out any slag that will not come off.
**Stagger** the starts and stops of each pass by at least 25 mm, so weak spots do not line up through the joint.
Before restarting from a crater, clear its slag and grind it to a smooth taper, so the new arc fuses into it.
Keep the interpass temperature inside the WPS range: measure it before each pass.
Lay straight stringers or narrow weaves as the WPS says; wide weaves out of position trap slag and give poor fusion.

blocks.p: A big fillet (for example 10–12 mm) cannot be laid in one pass: the metal would sag onto the bottom plate, giving uneven legs, overlap and poor fusion on the upright plate. Plan the beads in layers.

flow: Layer 1: one root bead into the corner, gun aimed at the root
Layer 2: the first bead along the bottom plate, overlapping about half the root bead; then a bead above it against the upright plate
Layer 3 (if needed): three beads, again starting at the bottom plate and working upward
Clean every bead before the next; stagger starts and stops
Measure both legs and the throat with a fillet gauge; check for undercut on the upright plate and overlap on the bottom plate

head: AWS
ISO
Position
rows: Overhead butt (4F, the overhead fillet, is PD)

head: Position
Technique
rows: Stringer beads only, laid from the **bottom** of the groove upward, each bead forming a shelf for the next; gun tilted slightly up (about 5–15°) so the pool does not sag; watch for undercut on the upper plate

Weld **uphill** with all-position rutile wire, with a small side-to-side or triangle weave, pausing at the edges; downhill welding with these wires risks lack of fusion and is used only where the WPS allows it
Small stringer beads, short stick-out, slightly lower settings; full PPE including head and neck protection
Highest deposit; weave or stringers as the WPS says

blocks.p: An open pipe root is hard to make with FCAW: the slag can be trapped inside the root and on the inside of the pipe. So the root (and often a second, hot pass) is usually welded with **GTAW** or short-circuit **GMAW**, which give a clean, even root, before the FCAW fill and cap.

flow: Prepare, fit and tack the pipe to the WPS; check gap and hi-lo
Weld the root with GTAW or GMAW, then a second pass so the root is thick enough not to burn through when FCAW starts
Clean the root and check it from inside with a mirror and light
Weld the FCAW fill passes uphill on each half (5G): start just past the bottom (6 o'clock) and finish just past the top (12 o'clock), changing the gun angle as you go round
Clean slag after every pass; stagger starts and stops
Lay the cap evenly, with no undercut; inspect inside and out

blocks.note: A macro section cut through a multi-process pipe joint shows whether the FCAW passes have fused into the GTAW or GMAW root. Look for a clean line of fusion with no slag between them.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: It needs three things together: **hydrogen** in the weld (from damp wire, gas, rust, oil, paint or humid air), a **hard structure** in the weld or HAZ (from high-strength or thick steel cooling fast), and **stress** from restraint. The cracks can appear hours after welding.

ul: Use a low-hydrogen wire (for example with an H4 or H8 mark) where the WPS names one, and keep wire sealed and dry.
Clean joints to bright metal.
Preheat to the WPS figure, and **preheat the tacks too**: small tacks cool very fast and can crack.
Keep the interpass temperature in range, and post-heat or cool slowly where the WPS says.
Because cracks can be delayed, final inspection of thick, high-strength welds is often done a set time after welding (often 16–48 hours), as the specification says.

blocks.p: A bead that is much **deeper than it is wide** freezes from both side walls towards the middle and pushes impurities to the centre, where it can split as it cools. It is common in deep, narrow root beads and narrow grooves at high current. Cure: a slightly wider, shallower bead (lower current, a little more voltage, a wider groove), and avoid concave root beads.

**Lamellar tearing** is a stepped crack inside a rolled plate, running parallel to its surface just below a weld. It happens in thick T-joints and corner joints where a large weld pulls on the plate **through its thickness**, opening thin layers of impurities in the steel.

head: Who
How to prevent it
rows: Change the joint so the weld does not pull through the plate's thickness; specify plate with a tested **through-thickness** property for critical joints; check thick plate for layers by ultrasonic testing before welding

**Butter** the face of the plate first (lay a layer of tough weld metal on it before the joint is made); use the smallest weld the drawing allows; low-hydrogen wire; preheat; a welding sequence that reduces restraint

blocks.p: Self-shielded flux-cored weld metal contains elements (such as aluminium) that the flux uses to protect the pool. When its passes are mixed with MMAW or gas-shielded passes in one joint, the mixed weld metal can lose toughness. Many specifications require such a combination to be tested before it is used.

ul: **Build-up** restores a worn part to near its old size with ordinary, tough weld metal (or a build-up wire).

**Hardfacing** lays a hard, wear-resistant layer, such as chromium-carbide, on top, usually no more than the two or three layers the maker allows. Hardfacing straight onto the worn part, or too many layers, can make the deposit spall off.

Many chromium-carbide deposits form fine **cross-checks** (relief cracks) across the bead as they cool. The maker's data says whether this is normal; cracks must not run into the build-up or the base metal.
Wear-resistant and high-carbon parts often need preheat, so that the HAZ and the build-up do not crack.
Double-V preparations, welded on each side in turn, keep plate flat.
Pre-set the parts against the expected pull.
On long members, weld balanced and from the centre outwards; use back-step or skip sequences.
Check flatness with a straight edge before welding and after each stage.

flow: Weld the first side and clean it

From the second side, gouge by grinding (or air carbon arc gouging, only where the Centre allows and under supervision) until **clean, sound weld metal** from the first side shows along the whole joint
Shape the groove into a smooth U that the next pass can fuse into; grind off any carbon-rich skin from gouging
Check the groove by eye, and by MT or PT if the WPS asks
Weld the second side

blocks.note: You have gone deep enough when sound, clean weld metal shows all along the groove: not at a set depth, and not when the disc is worn. Dark lines or pores mean you keep going.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Method
Use on FCAW work
rows: Every weld: size, profile, undercut, overlap, porosity, cracks, slag, spatter, arc strikes, craters
Quick and well suited to surface and near-surface cracks in carbon steel, including fillet welds
Surface cracks on any non-porous metal; used on **stainless** steel, which is not magnetic
Internal faults in butt welds, as the specification asks
A cut, polished and etched section shows fusion, penetration, bead order and fillet size

head: Fault
Likely causes
Cure
rows: Slag not cleaned between passes; convex beads; slag running ahead; wide weave
Clean every pass; drag angle; flatter beads; stringers
Too low current or voltage; too fast; wrong angle; downhill where not allowed
Settings in the WPS range; aim at the side walls; weld uphill
Gas blown away; damp or rusty wire; short stick-out on self-shielded wire; dirty joint
Screen draughts; dry wire; correct stick-out; clean joints
Voltage or speed too high; wrong angle in 2G or 2F
Lower voltage; gun angle; stringer order
Damp wire, no preheat, hard steel, restraint
Low-hydrogen wire, preheat and interpass control

flow: Mark the crack, report and record it
Find its full length with MT or PT, and its likely cause; check that a WPS covers the repair
Drill a small hole at each end if the procedure asks, then remove the crack by grinding or gouging, with sloping ends, to sound metal
Prove the crack is gone by MT or PT on the groove
Preheat if the WPS says, and re-weld with the approved wire and settings
After the waiting time the specification gives, inspect again by the same method, and record the repair

blocks.h: Cutting and etching a macro section

flow: Mark where the section is to be cut, away from the start and stop of the weld
Cut it with a saw (under supervision), never with a cutting torch, which would change the metal
File and grind the cut face flat, then rub it down on finer and finer abrasive papers
Etch it with the etching solution the Centre uses, wearing the gloves and eye protection its SDS names, in a ventilated place
Rinse, dry and read it: fusion into each plate and between passes, penetration, bead order, leg lengths and throat
Record the results and keep the section labelled with its joint number

blocks.p: Remove all slag and spatter before painting. Paint over slag soon flakes off and lets rust start underneath.

sections.title: Productivity, costing and leading the team

ul: **Fillet cross-section** ≈ leg × leg ÷ 2. A 9 mm fillet: 9 × 9 ÷ 2 = 40.5 mm².
**Volume per metre** = cross-section × 1 000 mm. 40.5 mm² gives 40 500 mm³ = 40.5 cm³ per metre.
**Mass** = volume × 7.85 g per cm³. 40.5 cm³ × 7.85 = 318 g, about 0.32 kg per metre.
**Wire needed** = weld metal ÷ wire efficiency. Gas-shielded FCAW wire efficiency is often about 80–90% (the rest is slag, spatter and stub ends).
**Wire per minute** = wire feed speed × mass per metre of wire. 1.2 mm cored wire weighs very roughly 7 g per metre, so 8 m/min uses about 56 g/min.
**Arc time** = weld metal ÷ deposition rate (kg of weld metal per hour of arc time).

**Operating factor** = arc time as a percentage of working time. 2.5 hours of arc in an 8-hour shift is 2.5 ÷ 8 = about 31%. Welders also fit, clean, move and wait, so in shops it is often about 25–50%.
**Labour time** = arc time ÷ operating factor. 2 hours of arc at 40% is 2 ÷ 0.4 = 5 hours.
**Shielding gas** = flow rate × arc time. 20 L/min for 2 hours of arc is 20 × 120 = 2 400 litres.

head: Worked example: 25 m of 9 mm fillet
Working
rows: 7.95 ÷ 0.85 = about 9.4 kg: order a 15 kg spool
2.3 ÷ 0.4 = about 5.7 hours, plus set-up and inspection

blocks.note: Costs in the examples are made up: use the shop's current prices for wire, gas and labour, in J$. For example, 12 kg of wire at J$1 250 per kg costs J$15 000.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Planning the time for a job

ul: Passes × (welding time + cleaning time): a butt needing 7 passes of 18 minutes, each followed by 4 minutes of cleaning, takes 7 × 22 = 154 minutes.
Total length of weld: a beam with 6 stiffeners, each with 4 fillets 300 mm long, has 6 × 4 × 0.3 = 7.2 m of fillet.
Wire per hour of arc: a 15 kg spool that lasts 6 hours of arc time is used at 15 ÷ 6 = 2.5 kg per hour.
At the start of the shift, check that the WPSs for the day's jobs are at the bays and that each welder is qualified for the process, positions and thickness.
Check machines, guns, liners, gas, extraction, and that the wire on each feeder is the class the WPS lists, dry and labelled. Keep different classes apart.
Make sure joints are fitted, cleaned and preheated before welding.
Check the first piece of each job fully before the rest are made.
Walk round during the day: watch technique, check slag cleaning and settings, and stop work outside the WPS.
Coach welders whose work shows faults: name the fault, its cause and the fix.
Record each weld with the welder, the wire batch and the inspection result; deal with faults through the proper repair route.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and work on it with your instructor.

ul: I can compare gas-shielded and self-shielded flux-cored wires and say where each suits.
I can read an FCAW classification such as E71T-1C or E81T1-Ni1C.
I can compare T-1, T-5, T-8, T-4 and T-11 wires and choose one for a job.
I can choose the right stainless wire for 304 to 304 and for stainless to carbon steel.
I can store and handle cored wire so that it stays dry and clean.
I can name the fume hazards of FCAW, including manganese and chromium, and control them.
I can set polarity, drive rolls, tip, stick-out, gas flow and settings, and fix common feed and gas problems.
I can read welding symbols, including arrow side, other side, intermittent welds, weld-all-round and field welds.
I can plan and weld a multi-pass 2F fillet and a 2G double-V butt.
I can weld uphill in 3G and overhead in 4G with the right technique.
I can explain how a pipe joint is made with a GTAW or GMAW root and FCAW fill and cap in 5G.
I can explain hydrogen cracking, centreline cracking and lamellar tearing, and how each is prevented.
I can explain buttering, build-up and hardfacing.
I can back gouge to sound metal and check the groove.
I can choose MT, PT, RT, UT or a macro for a job, and repair a crack so the repair is accepted.
I can work out weld metal, wire, arc time, labour time and gas for a job.
I can control quality across an FCAW crew.

terms: Build-up
Restoring a worn part to near its old size with ordinary weld metal
Buttering
Laying weld metal on a joint face before the joint is made
Carbon dioxide (CO2)
A shielding gas used on its own with many gas-shielded flux-cored wires
CTWD (stick-out)
The distance from the contact tip to the work
CVN
Charpy V-notch: an impact test of toughness
Deposition rate
Kilograms of weld metal laid per hour of arc time
Drag angle
Pointing the gun back towards the finished weld, so slag stays behind the pool
FCAW-G and FCAW-S
Gas-shielded and self-shielded flux-cored arc welding
Field weld
A weld made on site, shown by a flag on the welding symbol
Hardfacing
Welding a hard, wear-resistant layer onto a part
Lamellar tearing
A stepped crack inside a plate below a weld, caused by pull through the thickness
Manganese
A metal in welding fume that can harm the nervous system
Needle scaler
An air tool with steel needles for cleaning slag
Operating factor
Arc time as a percentage of working time
PB
The ISO position that matches AWS 2F, the horizontal fillet
Self-shielded wire
A flux-cored wire that needs no outside shielding gas
Solidification cracking
A crack down the centre of a bead that is deeper than it is wide
Usability type
The number after the T, which gives the wire's flux type, polarity and behaviour
Weld access hole
A hole cut in a beam web so the flange weld can be made right across
Wire efficiency
The share of the wire that ends up as weld metal

c1.title: Stainless brackets at a juice plant in Bog Walk
c1.text: Andrea's team is making a steel frame at a juice plant in Bog Walk, St Catherine. The frame is mild steel, but the brackets that touch the juice tanks are 304 stainless steel, and they are to be welded to the mild steel frame with flux-cored wire in a small, enclosed bay. The supervisor has asked for the welds on the stainless brackets to be checked for surface cracks.

c2.title: A telecom tower base near Mandeville
c2.text: Kirk's crew is welding the base frame of a steel tower on an open hilltop near Mandeville, Manchester, where strong winds blow most afternoons. The WPS names self-shielded E71T-8 wire, DCEN, for multi-pass fillets on 20 mm base plates, with a stick-out of 20–30 mm. One welder holds about 10 mm of stick-out 'for better control', and his welds show porosity. Another has brought a spool of E71T-11 from the store because 'it runs smoother'. The spool left on one feeder in the site container all week now has rust spots.

c3.title: Column splices for a parking deck in New Kingston
c3.text: Sean leads an FCAW crew making 2G double-V butt splices in 25 mm columns for a parking deck in New Kingston. The WPS names E71T-1C H8 wire with 100% CO2 on DCEP. A welder wants to change to a 75% argon / 25% CO2 mix 'for a smoother arc'. On one splice a crack is found running along the centre of a deep, narrow root bead. During long runs in the afternoon, the CO2 regulator frosts over and the flow drops.

c4.title: A worn loader bucket at a quarry near Lucea
c4.text: At a quarry near Lucea, Hanover, Clive must rebuild the worn cutting edge of a loader bucket. About 10 mm has worn away. The bucket maker's procedure calls for preheat, a build-up wire for the first layers, then two layers of a chromium-carbide hardfacing flux-cored wire. After the hardfacing cools, fine cracks run across each bead.

c5.title: Estimating stiffener welds for a girder in May Pen
c5.text: Tavia, a charge hand at a shop in May Pen, Clarendon, is estimating the FCAW work on a plate girder. It has 40 m of 6 mm fillet welds. The shop's figures are: wire efficiency about 80%, a deposition rate of 2.5 kg of weld metal per hour of arc time, an operating factor of 45%, and a gas flow of 18 litres per minute while the arc is on. Steel weighs 7.85 g per cm³.

questions.q: Which wire suits the stainless-to-mild-steel welds?
o: E71T-1C
questions.why: Type 309 filler has extra chromium and nickel, so it can take the dilution from the mild steel and still give a crack-resistant stainless weld. E308L suits 304 to 304, and a carbon steel wire would leave a weld that rusts and may crack.

questions.q: Which crack test suits the welds on the stainless brackets?
o: Magnetic particle testing
A hammer test on each weld
Hardness testing of the cap
Dye penetrant testing
questions.why: Type 304 stainless steel is not magnetic, so magnetic particle testing does not work on it. Dye penetrant testing finds cracks open to the surface on any non-porous metal.

questions.q: Why does the stainless welding in the enclosed bay need extra fume control?
o: Its fume has chromium compounds that can cause cancer
Stainless fume is heavier, so it lies along the floor
Stainless wire flux gives off nothing but carbon monoxide
Stainless fume is harmless but has a very strong smell
questions.why: Welding stainless steel gives off fume containing hexavalent chromium, which harms the lungs and can cause cancer. Local exhaust at the arc and the respirator the risk assessment names are needed, especially in an enclosed bay.

questions.q: What is the most likely cause of the porosity in the first welder's work?
o: Wind blowing the gas from the shielding cylinder
DCEN polarity, which always gives some porosity
Stick-out far shorter than the maker's range
Base plates too thick for flux-cored wire to weld
questions.why: Self-shielded wires are designed to run at the maker's stick-out: the extra length preheats the wire so the flux can protect the pool. Too short a stick-out is a common cause of porosity. There is no gas cylinder with this wire.

questions.q: Why should Kirk stop the E71T-11 being used on these fillets?
o: It needs a shielding gas, which cannot be used here
It can only be used in the flat welding position
It is limited to thinner work and is not on the WPS
It is a stainless steel wire, not a carbon steel wire
questions.why: E71T-11 is a general-purpose self-shielded wire with limits on plate thickness and no toughness rating, so it does not suit multi-pass structural fillets on 20 mm plate. Only the class the WPS names may be used.

questions.q: What should be done about the spool with rust spots?
o: Take it off and fit a clean spool stored as the maker says
Run it at a higher voltage so the rust burns off in the arc
Wipe the wire with an oily rag as it feeds into the gun
Use it for the root passes, where nobody will see it
questions.why: Rust and moisture on cored wire feed badly and add porosity and hydrogen. The spool is taken out of use, and spools are kept covered or bagged off the feeder when not in use, as the maker says.

questions.q: What is the problem with changing to the argon-CO2 mix?
o: Argon mixes cannot be used with any flux-cored wire
Argon mixes always cause porosity with cored wire
None, as long as the flow rate stays the same
The WPS and wire class cover CO2, not the mix
questions.why: The C in E71T-1C shows the wire was classified with CO2. With an argon mix more manganese and silicon reach the weld, raising strength and lowering toughness. A gas change is a WPS change, so it is made only if a WPS covers it and the wire is classified for it (an M designation).

questions.q: What most likely caused the crack along the centre of the root bead?
o: The travel speed on the root was too slow
The bead was much deeper than it was wide
The CO2 flow was set too high for the root
The voltage was set too high for the root
questions.why: A deep, narrow bead freezes from both side walls towards the middle and pushes impurities there, so it can split as it cools (solidification cracking). A slightly wider, shallower root bead avoids it.

questions.q: In the 2G position, in what order should the fill passes be laid?
o: From the bottom of the groove upward
From the top of the groove downward
One wide weave across the groove each layer
Top and bottom edges first, middle last
questions.why: Each stringer laid from the lower side wall upward forms a shelf that supports the next, so the pool does not sag. A wide weave in 2G sags onto the lower plate and undercuts the upper one.

questions.q: Why does the CO2 regulator frost over on long runs, and what is the fix?
o: Humid air freezes on it; wrap it in a cloth while welding
The cylinder is nearly empty; turn the flow up to make up
Fast boil-off chills it; use a heated regulator
The gas is the wrong type; change to pure argon instead
questions.why: CO2 is stored as a liquid, and boiling it off fast cools the cylinder and regulator until they freeze and the flow drops. A heated regulator, or several cylinders on a manifold, keeps the supply steady.

questions.q: In what order should the layers go on?
o: Hardfacing first, then build-up on top to protect it
Build-up to near size, then the hardfacing layers
Hardfacing all the way, to fill the whole 10 mm
Build-up and hardfacing beads laid side by side
questions.why: Hardfacing alloys are hard and brittle and are meant as thin top layers. The worn edge is first built back up with tough build-up metal, then capped with the number of hardfacing layers the maker gives.

questions.q: What do the fine cracks across the chromium-carbide beads usually mean?
o: The bucket edge must be scrapped and replaced
Hydrogen cracks that need a full repair at once
The build-up layers were left out by mistake
Normal relief checks, if the maker says so
questions.why: Many chromium-carbide overlays form fine cross-checks as they cool, which relieve stress and are accepted by the maker. Cracks must not run down into the build-up or the base metal, so the maker's data decides what is acceptable.

questions.q: Why does the procedure call for preheat on the bucket edge?
o: Preheat makes the hardfacing softer to grind
Preheat dries the flux inside the wire as it feeds
Preheat is only to burn the old paint off the edge
The hard edge steel could crack if it cools fast
questions.why: Bucket edges are often hard, wear-resistant steel. Preheat slows cooling, lowers the hardness of the HAZ and reduces the risk of cracks starting in the base metal or the build-up.

questions.q: Using the shop's figures, what mass of deposited steel do Tavia's 40 m of 6 mm fillets hold?
o: About 11.3 kg
About 5.7 kg
About 0.14 kg
About 7.1 kg
questions.why: Cross-section = 6 × 6 ÷ 2 = 18 mm², which is 18 cm³ per metre, or 18 × 7.85 = 141 g per metre. For 40 m that is about 5.7 kg. 11.3 kg forgets to halve, 0.14 kg is one metre, and 7.1 kg is the wire, not the weld metal.

questions.q: About how many hours of labour should Tavia allow for the welding?
o: About 2.3 hours
About 1 hour
About 5 hours
About 7 hours
questions.why: Arc time = 5.65 ÷ 2.5 = about 2.3 hours. With an operating factor of 45%, labour = 2.3 ÷ 0.45 = about 5 hours, before set-up and inspection. 2.3 hours is arc time only, and 1 hour multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.q: About how much shielding gas will the job use?
o: About 2 400 litres
About 41 litres
About 5 400 litres
About 1 100 litres
questions.why: Gas flows only while the arc burns: about 2.26 hours × 60 = 136 minutes × 18 L/min = about 2 400 litres. 5 400 litres wrongly uses the labour time, and 41 litres forgets to change hours into minutes.

questions.q: Flux-cored wire comes out of the gun flattened, and flux powder gathers in the feeder. What should be checked first?
o: The gas flow: turn it up to blow the powder clear
The drive rolls: knurled rolls at a lighter pressure
The contact tip: fit one a size smaller to hold the wire
The liner: grease it so the wire slides more easily
questions.why: Cored wire is a thin tube. Smooth V rolls or too much pressure crush it, opening the seam and spilling flux. Knurled (or the maker's cored-wire) rolls grip it with light pressure.

questions.q: A drawing shows a fillet symbol with 6 on its left and 50-150 on its right. What does it ask for?
o: 6 mm fillets, 50 mm long at 150 mm centres
6 fillets, each from 50 mm to 150 mm long
6 mm fillets with 50 mm gaps and 150 mm welds
A 6 mm fillet between 50 mm and 150 mm wide
questions.why: The size goes to the left of the symbol and the length and pitch to the right: 50 mm welds whose centres are 150 mm apart, each with a 6 mm leg. Reading it wrong either wastes wire or leaves the joint under-welded.

questions.q: A WPS for structural fillets with an all-position rutile wire says 3F uphill. A welder wants to weld downhill because it is faster. Why is this not allowed?
o: Downhill welds use far more wire than uphill welds
Downhill welding is only allowed on stainless steel
It risks lack of fusion, and the WPS says uphill
Downhill welds cannot be cleaned of their slag
questions.why: Downhill, the slag and pool run ahead of the arc and the weld can lie on the plate without fusing. The WPS was qualified uphill, so the direction of travel cannot be changed without a procedure that covers it.

questions.q: On a welding symbol, what does a small flag at the bend of the arrow mean?
o: The weld must be ground flush after welding
The weld goes all the way round the joint
The weld is to be inspected by radiography
The weld is made on site, not in the shop
questions.why: The flag marks a field weld, made on site during erection. Knowing which welds are shop welds and which are field welds lets the team leader plan the wire, equipment, WPS and crew for each place.
